00. Overview & Learning Objectives

  • Describe Chapman's reflexes (Chapman's points), including how they form
  • Find anterior and posterior Chapman's points related to the GI, GU, and cardiac systems — treatment does not usually require special positioning
  • Discuss how Chapman's reflexes are used clinically, including narrowing a differential diagnosis
  • Describe the characteristics of and palpatory differences between Chapman's points, counterstrain (tender) points, and Travell's trigger points
Reading: Foundations of Osteopathic Medicine, 4th ed. (Seffinger, ed.), Ch. 10 Autonomic Nervous System by Frank Willard, pp. 221–230 & 247–252, Table 10.1 p. 254. Supplemental: ScholarRx Bricks on Spinal Facilitation and Chapman's Points.

01. What Are Chapman's Points?

  • Described in the early 1900s by Frank Chapman, DO — originally called "Chapman's reflexes," later "Chapman's Reflex Points," now simply Chapman's points
  • Present in predictable places and groupings on the front and back of the body, related to dysfunction of specific organs and/or organ functions
  • A system of reflex points presenting as predictable anterior and posterior fascial tissue texture abnormalities, assumed to reflect visceral dysfunction or pathology
  • Though the term didn't exist yet at the time, what Chapman described is a form of viscerosomatic reflex — used to both diagnose and treat visceral pathology
  • There is almost always a related anterior point and a posterior point for each organ/system

Later refinement: Paul Kimberly, DO (1970s)

Correlated these neural lymphatic points (which he termed cutaneous lymphatic bundles) to anterior and lateral cutaneous nerves related to facilitated spinal segments — i.e., the facilitated segment sends signals down these cutaneous nerves, causing congestion/conglomeration of lymphatic, sensory, and nervous tissue.

Clinical note: Chapman's points are used more often as a diagnostic tool today than as a treatment target.
Practice Question

02. Mechanism: The Viscerosomatic Reflex

Proposed mechanism, in sequence:

  1. Visceral dysfunction
  2. → Facilitation (of the spinal cord segment)
  3. → Excessive sympathetic (SANS) tone
  4. → Focal lymphatic stasis / myofascial contraction
  5. → Somatic dysfunction (palpable as the Chapman's point)
Key concept: A Chapman's reflex point is therefore a somatic manifestation of a visceral problem — the palpable finding is downstream of organ dysfunction, not the cause of it.

03. T.A.R.T. Findings & Palpatory Characteristics

  • Predictable T.A.R.T. findings — the most common and prominent is tenderness, often quite significant before and during treatment
  • Manifest as "gangliform" contractions/nodules or excessive tissue congestion, sometimes with softer points on either side
  • Palpable bundles of lymphatic and vascular tissue and nerve endings, usually deep to the skin and subcutaneous tissue — most often within the deep fascia or the periosteum of bone
  • Located over the transverse processes posteriorly, and in the intercostal spaces anteriorly

Descriptive keywords

TermMeaning
RopeyA very short, fibrous rope
BoggyFeels as if it wants to pull the palpating finger further in
ShottyLike buckshot or birdshot
ThickenedFirm, congested tissue texture
Size: Classically described as the size of a dried pea or a grain of quinoa (~2–3 mm), but can range up to ~9 mm in diameter — roughly the width of a finger, or "pinhead to almond" sized.

04. Anterior vs. Posterior Points & Clinical Use

PointTypical Clinical Role
Anterior pointsUsually easier to access; commonly used for diagnosis
Posterior pointsMore often used for treatment, usually after balancing the pelvis
Most effective treatment utilizes both anterior and posterior points together.

Full-body reference charts (OPP I & II Manual appendix)

05. Chapman's Points vs. Trigger Points vs. Counterstrain

Each point type is treated differently — counterstrain and trigger points are usually used for treatment, while Chapman's points are more often used for diagnosis.

Point TypeOriginator / Treated WithRadiation?Shape / Tissue Texture
Chapman's point Frank Chapman, DO — rotatory stimulation for 20–60 seconds No Gangliform, granular, contracted, edematous, ropy, fibrospongy. Size from pinhead to almond (often pea-sized). May or may not be tender. Well-localized.
Trigger point Janet Travell, PT — injection, dry needling, ischemic compression, post-isometric relaxation MET, spray-and-stretch, or counterstrain Yes — in reproducible patterns Distinct nodules ("knots") in muscle, or a rope-like "taut band" at the tendon. Size similar to a Chapman's point. Tender and localized (with radiation).
Counterstrain point (tenderpoint) Larry Jones, DO — counterstrain No Discrete, small, tense, edematous. Size of a fingertip. Very tender and localized.
Practice Question

06. Treatment Technique & Sequencing

  • Treatment consists of gentle vibratory or circulatory (rotatory) pressure on the point — classically for 20–60 seconds
  • Anterior and posterior points are ideally treated simultaneously, for the time it takes the point(s) to resolve or disappear
  • Balance the pelvis first: Chapman himself stated treatment of these points should not begin until all somatic dysfunctions in the pelvis have been resolved ("balancing the pelvis")
  • Treatment can be performed without this step, but effects are less durable if the pelvis is not balanced first
  • Chapman traditionally ended a treatment session once the affected points had been treated

07. Key Points: GI/GU/Abdominal Systems

Anterior points for a given organ system are usually physically close together, mirroring their real anatomic relationships.

OrganAnteriorPosterior
AppendixTip of the right 12th ribTransverse process of T11, right side
Adrenals2" superior and 1" lateral to the umbilicusBetween spinous & transverse processes of T11–T12
Kidneys1" superior and 1" lateral to the umbilicus (inferior/medial to adrenal points)Between spinous & transverse processes of T12–L1
BladderPeriumbilical region—
ColonLateral thigh, within the iliotibial band, from the greater trochanter to just above the knee. Imagine the path of the large intestine mirrored onto the thighs: ascending colon points are on the right lateral thigh (beginning of ascending colon closer to the greater trochanter, proximal 2/3 of transverse colon closer to the knee); descending colon points mirror onto the left thigh.
Relative anatomy pearl: Bladder points are near the umbilicus; kidney points sit superior and lateral to the bladder points; adrenal points sit superior to the kidney points — the anterior map mirrors the actual retroperitoneal anatomy.
Practice Question

08. Key Points: Cardiac & Upper GI (IC Space Reference)

OrganAnteriorPosterior
Myocardium (heart)2nd intercostal space (ICS), close to the sternumIntertransverse space between T2–T3
Liver5th ICS, right (near sternum); also 6th ICS, right (with gallbladder)Not separately emphasized from gallbladder posteriorly
Gallbladder6th ICS, from the mid-clavicular line (MCL) to the sternum, rightIntertransverse space between T6–T7, right
Stomach — hyperacidity5th ICS, from MCL to sternum, leftIntertransverse space between T5–T6, left
Stomach/duodenum — peristalsis (decreased motility)6th ICS, from MCL to sternum, leftIntertransverse space between T6–T7, left
Pancreas7th ICS, right, near the costochondral junctionIntertransverse space between T7–T8
Spleen7th ICS, left (mirrors pancreas on the right)—

Quick IC-space mnemonic (Kuchera, p. 90)

Intercostal SpaceRightLeft
5th ICSLiverStomach (acid)
6th ICSLiver, gallbladderStomach (peristalsis)
7th ICSPancreasSpleen
Laterality pearl: Gallbladder, liver, and pancreas points are on the right; stomach and spleen points are on the left — following normal organ laterality.
Practice Question

09. Clinical Case: Patient AB

History

AB is a 44-year-old obese female presenting with severe, colicky right-sided abdominal pain. She is diaphoretic. The pain began immediately after eating a large, spicy, cheesy meal. She has had similar pain before after spicy or fatty meals, but this episode is much worse than usual. She has gone through 6–7 rolls of OTC antacids per week for the past 5 years, but they haven't helped this time. She has taken lisinopril 40 mg daily for 6 years (for hypertension). She is worried because she has heard women don't always experience heart attacks the way men do — her father died at age 48 of a massive heart attack while playing tennis.

Physical Exam

  • HR 85, RR 18, BP 165/95
  • Cardiac: regular rate, normal S1/S2
  • Pulmonary: clear to auscultation bilaterally
  • Abdomen: positive tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant; decreased bowel sounds in all four quadrants
  • Musculoskeletal/OMM findings: OA FRRSL; C3 & C4 ERSL; T6–T9 NSRRL; left-on-left sacral torsion; right innominate anteriorly rotated
  • 2–3 mm gangliform mass on the right, near the sternum, in the 6th intercostal space (positive gallbladder Chapman's point)
  • Myocardium Chapman's point (2nd ICS / T2–T3 intertransverse space) — negative/absent

Differential diagnosis

DiagnosisSupporting history/exam
Cholecystitis / cholelithiasis (top of list)RUQ pain, worse after a spicy/fatty meal; classic "4 F's" — Forty, Female, Fat, Fertile
Stomach ulcerRelated to eating; pain can be substernal or epigastric, though classically LUQ rather than RUQ
Acute MIMust stay on the differential — women often present atypically (severe indigestion, sense of impending doom, rather than classic chest/arm pain); family history of early (<50) cardiac death; hypertension (though BP elevation here could simply reflect pain/anxiety)
ConstipationDecreased bowel sounds in all four quadrants; cramping from constipation can be colicky and diffuse
AppendicitisAtypical presentations exist — an anatomically higher-positioned appendix can cause RUQ rather than RLQ pain

How Chapman's points inform the diagnosis

  • Gallbladder point positive (6th ICS, right, MCL-to-sternum / posterior T6–T7 intertransverse) — supports cholecystitis
  • Myocardium point negative (2nd ICS / T2–T3 intertransverse) — makes acute MI less likely, though cardiac labs are still appropriately ordered given her risk factors and atypical-presentation concern
  • Net effect: reasonable to pursue a RUQ ultrasound rather than immediate activation of the cath lab — while still not ignoring the cardiac risk
Teaching point: This case illustrates the core clinical use of Chapman's points — checking multiple relevant points (not just the one that "fits") to help narrow, rule in, or rule out entries on a differential, alongside (not instead of) standard workup.
